\section[sensible]{sensible — sensitive}

\label{lesson:ES-C727-sensible}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for modest, then the Spanish for to show off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sensible}
\textbf{sensible} — \textquotedblleft{}sensitive\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es un chico muy sensible.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is a very sensitive boy.}
\end{quote}

A false friend: sensible is \emph{sensato}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sensible} comes from Latin \emph{sēnsibilis} \textquotedblleft{}having feeling\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{sentīre} \textquotedblleft{}to feel\textquotedblright{}; Spanish kept the feeling sense.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sensible}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sensible}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{sensible}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for modest, then the Spanish for to show off, then say \emph{sensible} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does sensible mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Sensitive\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sensibilidad]{la sensibilidad — sensitivity}

\label{lesson:ES-C727-sensibilidad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to show off, then the Spanish for sensitive.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la sensibilidad}
\textbf{la sensibilidad} — \textquotedblleft{}sensitivity\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tiene mucha sensibilidad para la música.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She has a great feel for music.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sensibilidad} comes from Latin \emph{sēnsibilitās} (EtymDB), built on \emph{sēnsibilis}, from \emph{sentīre} \textquotedblleft{}to feel\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[ofender]{ofender — to offend}

\label{lesson:ES-C727-ofender}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for sensitive, then the Spanish for sensitivity.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ofender}
\textbf{ofender} — \textquotedblleft{}to offend\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No quería ofenderte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I did not want to offend you.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ofenderse} — to take offence.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ofender} comes from Latin \emph{offendere} \textquotedblleft{}to strike against\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{ob} \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[educado]{educado — polite, well-mannered}

\label{lesson:ES-C727-educado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for sensitivity, then the Spanish for to offend.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: educado}
\textbf{educado} — \textquotedblleft{}polite, well-mannered\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tus hijos son muy educados.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Your children are very polite.}
\end{quote}

A false friend: it means polite, not only educated. \emph{Maleducado} is rude.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{educado} is the participle of \emph{educar}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ēducāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bring up, to rear\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{educado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{educado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{educado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for sensitivity, then the Spanish for to offend, then say \emph{educado} again
\end{itemize}

\section[grosero]{grosero — rude, coarse}

\label{lesson:ES-C727-grosero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to offend, then the Spanish for polite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: grosero}
\textbf{grosero} — \textquotedblleft{}rude, coarse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No seas grosero con la camarera.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not be rude to the waitress.}
\end{quote}

Also vulgar: \emph{una palabra grosera}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{grosero} is built on \emph{grueso} \textquotedblleft{}thick\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{grossus} \textquotedblleft{}thick, coarse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); rough cloth became rough manners.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
